planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil has warmed past 70°F; Honeyshaw ripens roughly a week to ten days earlier than standard Crenshaw, which makes it a workable choice for gardeners outside the hottest, longest-summer regions where true Crenshaw struggles to finish.

directions: Honeyshaw was introduced by Petoseed Company around 1980 as an earlier-ripening, Crenshaw-type melon bred for growers in the sunbelt who wanted Crenshaw's rich flavor without the full 90-110 day commitment the classic heirloom demands. Fruits are medium-sized with ribbed skin that shifts from dark green toward yellow as they mature, and the pastel-pink-to-orange flesh carries a sweet, distinctive flavor reminiscent of its Crenshaw parentage. Plant in hills of three to four seeds in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, and keep moisture even through flowering and early fruit set before easing back as fruit ripens to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the blossom end softens slightly and the rind's green cast has given way to yellow, since Honeyshaw loses its characteristic aroma quickly once overripe.
sources: NC State University Cucurbit Breeding Program — Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America
Harvest to Table — Growing Galia, Honeydew, and Crenshaw Melons

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early in short-season gardens, in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; space plants 18-24 inches apart in rows 4-6 feet apart.

directions: Golden Crispy is a small Japanese melon that built a following as a commercial gourmet variety before disappearing from catalogs in the early 1980s; seed was later tracked down and reintroduced by specialty heirloom growers. The smooth, golden-skinned fruit are oblong to pear-shaped and notably small, averaging about half a pound each, which lets a single vine set an unusually high number of melons for its size. The white flesh is crisp rather than soft-textured, with a sweet, distinctively aromatic flavor that sets it apart from typical musky cantaloupe types. Grow it like other melons in warm, fertile soil with consistent deep watering through fruit development, switching to drip or soil-level irrigation to limit the foliar disease that overhead watering invites.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Golden Crispy Melon
Smart Gardener — Melon: Golden Crispy Growing Guide

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-drained soil; this variety is adapted to the hot, dry growing conditions of Rajasthan and performs best where summers are long and intensely hot.

directions: Madhu Ras, meaning "honey nectar" in Hindi, is a small-fruited heirloom muskmelon still grown in home gardens and local markets across Rajasthan, India, and was brought into North American seed trade after being collected at a Delhi market by plant explorer Joseph Simcox. The compact fruit are yellow with green striping and weigh roughly one to one and a half pounds, with soft, silky, intensely sweet orange flesh carrying a classic muskmelon aroma. Because it evolved under the hot, arid conditions of western India, it tolerates heat and drier soil better than many Western cantaloupe types, though fruiting and sweetness both improve with regular watering once fruit begins to set. Harvest at full slip, when the stem releases cleanly from the fruit with light pressure, for the best sugar content and aroma.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Madhu Ras, Rajasthan Honey Melon
Experimental Farm Network — Joseph Simcox heirloom melon collections

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early where the growing season is short; Golden Honeymoon ripens roughly two weeks ahead of standard green-fleshed honeydew types.

directions: Golden Honeymoon is a honeydew-type heirloom prized for combining a brilliant gold rind with the classic pale green flesh of honeydew melon, maturing roughly two weeks earlier than standard honeydew selections. Fruit reach three to five pounds, round and smooth-skinned, with juicy flesh that holds the mild, sweet flavor honeydew fans expect without the long, heat-hungry season many winter melons require. Because it finishes earlier than most inodorus-type melons, it is a practical choice for gardeners in cooler or shorter-summer regions who still want a true honeydew experience. Water deeply once or twice a week, keeping the soil evenly moist through fruit set, and harvest when the rind's gold color deepens and the blossom end yields slightly to thumb pressure.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Golden Honeymoon Melon
True Leaf Market — Golden Honeymoon Melon Seeds
Albert Lea Seed — Golden Honeymoon Melon

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-drained soil, or set 2-3 plants per hill; Sakata's Sweet has shown good tolerance of powdery mildew and fusarium wilt relative to many older open-pollinated melon types.

directions: Sakata's Sweet is an East Asian heirloom melon grown for centuries across the region before Sakata Seed Company in Japan rebranded and introduced it more widely; it has since been picked up by a handful of North American heirloom seed sellers. Fruit are small, oval to round, about the size of a baseball at ten to twelve ounces, with pale white-green skin that ripens to yellow-green and soft, barely green flesh that is smooth and notably sweet rather than strongly musky. The compact vines still sprawl in typical melon fashion but the modest fruit size makes it a good fit for smaller trellised plantings or raised beds. Grow on well-draining, fertile loam with consistent moisture at the soil line, and harvest as the skin fully yellows and develops a sweet fragrance at the blossom end.
sources: True Leaf Market — Sakata's Sweet Melon Seeds
Specialty Produce — Sakata Melons Information and Facts
